subject: Biology
title: Genetic Testing
description: A quick, practical guide to Genetic Testing.

hook.text: A simple blood test or cheek swab can reveal whether you carry genes for certain diseases.

buildup.text: Carrier screening checks if parents could pass conditions like cystic fibrosis to children.

discovery.text: Prenatal testing can detect chromosomal conditions like Down syndrome before birth.

twist.text: Direct-to-consumer DNA kits estimate disease risk, but the results are probabilities, not certainties.

climax.text: Knowing your genetic risks can guide prevention, but it also raises anxiety and privacy concerns.

punchline.text: Your DNA can warn you—if you want to listen.

quiz.question: What does carrier screening test for?
options: Whether parents carry genes for certain diseases

details.summary: Genetic testing analyzes DNA to detect mutations associated with disease, carrier status, drug responses, and ancestry. Tests range from prenatal screening and newborn panels to pharmacogenomics that guide medication choices based on an individual's genetic profile.
details.whyItMatters: Genetic testing enables personalized medicine by predicting disease risk before symptoms appear and guiding treatment choices. It empowers individuals with information but also raises challenges about interpretation and psychological impact.
takeaways: Carrier testing identifies people who carry disease alleles without symptoms
Pharmacogenomics tailors medication choices to individual genetic profiles
Direct-to-consumer tests provide health risk information with varying accuracy

faq.question: Should everyone get genetic testing?
faq.answer: It depends on personal and family circumstances. Testing is most valuable when there is a known family history of genetic disease, when pregnant, or when choosing medications. Genetic counselors help assess whether testing is appropriate and interpret results.

faq.question: How reliable are direct-to-consumer genetic tests?
faq.answer: Clinical-grade tests from medical labs are highly accurate. Consumer tests vary in quality and scope. They screen for limited variants and may miss important mutations. Positive results from consumer tests should always be confirmed by clinical testing.
